evidence_quotes.quote: The present study carried out in this city aimed at realizing a diagnosis of drinking water supply and basic sanitation services. To do so, we carried out semi-structured interviews, “focus groups”, household surveys and a documentary analysis of the institutional framework.

L’analyse du cadre institutionnel révèle que : les rôles des différents acteurs ne sont pas clairement définis et se recoupent très souvent. Il n’existe pas de plateforme de collaboration entre ces acteurs impliqués.
We found from this work that insufficient funds and the absence of electric power are the main problems of the actors of supply and demand of water and sanitation services.
En zone urbaine, les données ont été collectées à travers un questionnaire administré à 200 ménages choisis au hasard dans la ville.

71% of the population use borehole water without any previous treatment, 47% of households use improved pit latrines for sanitation. Although 69% of households were satisfied with basic sanitation, 74% were not satisfied with the drinking water supply. 36% of boreholes equipped with hand pumps were non-functional.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water supply and basic sanitation service access in the municipality of Kye-Ossi, South Cameroon, which lacks a public piped water network and municipal sanitation/emptying service.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study explicitly reviews the local institutional framework (identifying ministerial delegations and the municipal council under decentralization, noting unclear/overlapping institutional mandates, absence of an inter-actor collaboration platform, COGES water-point management issues, municipal vs. private public-latrine functionality, and non-compliance with borehole construction specifications). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, the study is a generic municipal infrastructure and service-delivery baseline diagnostic focused on hardware inventory, demographic projections of 2030 infrastructure needs, funding and electricity shortages, pump breakdowns, and macro-institutional background; it does not empirically analyze any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, eligibility, tenure/documentation, tariff/cost-recovery, enforcement, or ownership mechanism directly governing household access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a mixed-methods municipal diagnostic combining a random questionnaire survey of 200 urban households, rural village focus group discussions, semi-structured interviews with municipal sector officials and social institutions, documentary review, and a GPS-mapped census of water points and public latrines.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household drinking-water sources, latrine types, household satisfaction with water and sanitation services, collection distances (>2 km), retail water and public-toilet prices (100 FCFA per 20 L; 50-100 FCFA per toilet use), and functionality rates of boreholes, wells, and public latrines.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (200 urban households, rural village groups, social institutions, and 33 boreholes, 7 wells, and 7 public latrines in Kye-Ossi), broad municipal supply/institutional conditions, access/functionality outcomes, and a cross-sectional mixed-methods diagnostic case study design (though lacking a qualifying rule-type exposure under narrow Criterion 2).
criterion_notes.c6: Published in French with an English title and abstract; per Inclusion Criterion 10, direct translation/assessment from the provided French full text is straightforward and feasible (AI bilingual full-text reading), though the study is excluded on Criterion 2 (E03).

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods municipal case study / baseline diagnostic (household survey, semi-structured interviews, focus groups, documentary institutional review, GPS facility census, and demographic infrastructure projection)
population_and_sample: Municipality of Kye-Ossi, South Cameroon (estimated 75,000 inhabitants): 200 randomly selected urban households, rural village focus groups, semi-structured interviews with municipal sector officials and social institutions (schools, health centres, markets, religious establishments), and GPS census of 33 hand-pump boreholes, 7 modern wells, and 7 pay-per-use public latrines
exposure: Decentralized municipal institutional and supply-demand context (absence of public piped network and latrine-emptying service, overlapping institutional mandates and lack of inter-agency coordination platform, municipal funding and electricity shortages, equipment maintenance deficits); no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism examined
outcome: Household drinking-water sources (40% boreholes, 17% wells, 6% springs; 71% using borehole water untreated), household sanitation type (33% improved pit latrines, 25% unimproved pit latrines, 12% modern latrines), service satisfaction (26% satisfied with drinking water supply, 69% with basic sanitation), collection distance (>2 km), and infrastructure functionality (21/33 hand-pump boreholes functional, 7/7 modern wells functional, 4/4 private and 2/3 municipal public latrines functional)
rationale: This French-language empirical study (with an English abstract) conducts a mixed-methods baseline diagnostic of drinking-water and basic sanitation services in Kye-Ossi, South Cameroon, to inform a future municipal strategy. While it examines water and sanitation access (c1), collects primary survey, interview, focus-group, and GPS facility data (c3), and reports access, satisfaction, and functionality outcomes (c4), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification (excluded as E03, Wrong exposure). Although the paper passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 by reviewing the local institutional landscape (noting overlapping agency roles, lack of a coordination platform, decentralization constraints, COGES issues, and municipal vs. private public-toilet functionality), its focus is generic municipal service-delivery diagnosis, financial/electricity constraints, equipment breakdowns, and 2030 hardware projections rather than any legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access.
